newsitem.title: POLAND: Clinton tells Poles NATO offers power of peace.
newsitem.headline: Clinton tells Poles NATO offers power of peace.

text.p: Standing in a historic square in the city where the Warsaw Pact was born, U.S. President Bill Clinton on Thursday welcomed Poland's expected entry into NATO as a chance to create a new Europe through "the power of peace."

In a toast at the presidential palace, Clinton said the NATO invitation to Poland, Hungary and the Czech Republic to start talks on joining the alliance means "the old dividing lines of Europe were wiped away forever."
Instead, "we are building a framework of a Europe whole and free," he said.

Earlier, in Warsaw's Castle Square where thousands of Poles turned out to celebrate an epilogue to the final chapter of the Cold War, Clinton told the nation that has suffered so many foreign occupations and invasions that its people had earned their right to security.
"Never again will your fate be decided by others," Clinton said. "Never again will the birthright of freedom be denied you. Poland is coming home."

Clinton flew to Poland from Madrid, where NATO leaders invited the three nations to join an alliance forged nearly 50 years ago to counter the threat posed by the then-Soviet Union and the Warsaw Pact alliance that Poles had to be part of until they toppled communist rule in 1989.
"From this day forward, what Poland builds in peace, Poland will keep in security," said Clinton.
He said the contemporary world offers "history's most precious gift -- a second chance ... to unite Europe not by the force of arms, but by the power of peace."
Clinton stressed the responsibilities and burdens that come with NATO membership, including paying for defence and nurturing democracy.

"Now we must adapt our alliance to a new time," Clinton declared. "Our common enemy of communist oppression has vanished, but common dangers have not." He cited threats from terrorism, extreme nationalism and illegal drugs as well as the harm caused by ethnic, racial and religious hatreds.
Poland's President Aleksander Kwasniewski, a former communist who has embraced democracy, accepted that NATO entry implied obligations.
"The invitation to NATO is an accomplishment, but at the same time it is a challenge," he said. "We are all aware of the tasks ahead of us and the cost. Security does not come free."

On Friday, Clinton faces the delicate diplomatic mission of visiting Romania, which along with Slovenia had pressed hard to be admitted to NATO and now much content itself with waiting for the next round of expansion.

The first U.S. presidential visit to Bucharest in more than 20 years was designed as a gesture designed to soften the impact of Washington's objections to the immediate admission of Romania to the alliance.
Officials said Clinton wanted to stress that the United States was open to adding additional members to NATO and that Romania would be a leading contender if it continued on its road of reform.
Clinton plans private talks with President Emil Constaninescu and will deliver an outdoor address at University Square in Bucharest.
U.S. Ambassador to Romania Alfred Moses told Reuters earlier:
"He (Clinton) is going to Poland to congratulate the Poles, he's coming to Romania to say Romania is on the doorstep to joining NATO and that the door will remain open."
Clinton flies to Copenhagen on Friday night and will spend Saturday in Denmark before departing for Washington.
